szoveg_eredeti:
“Bad quality” is not one problem. A photo can be too small, out of focus, grainy, too dark, or crushed by compression, and each of those has a different fix. Run the wrong fix and you make it worse: sharpening a noisy photo sharpens the noise, and upscaling a blurry photo gives you a bigger blurry photo.

So the fastest way to improve photo quality is to name the problem first, then apply the one fix that matches it. This guide walks through the five common causes, how to spot each one, and how to fix it, both when you take the photo and after the fact with AI tools.

Left: a photo ruined by motion blur. Right: the same photo after one pass of Krea’s unblur tool. The rider, the bike and the street stay the same; the blur is gone.

Most bad photos have two of these at once. A night photo sent over a messaging app, for example, is usually noisy, compressed and small. Fix them in this order: blur, then resolution, noise and compression, then light.

A photo with too few pixels looks fine as a thumbnail and falls apart when you crop it, print it, or view it full screen. Classic resizing (bicubic in Photoshop, or “resize” in a phone editor) only stretches the pixels you have, so the result is bigger but just as soft.

An AI upscaler works differently: it predicts the detail that should be there, so edges, hair, text and textures come back sharp at the larger size.

The example from Krea’s Enhance page: a pixelated input and the enhanced result.

The free plan includes basic upscaling to 2K; paid plans go up to 22K for large prints, per krea.ai/pricing.

How many pixels do you need? For a sharp print, aim for 300 pixels per inch: 1200 × 1800 for a 4 × 6 in print, 2400 × 3000 for 8 × 10 in. For screens, match the display: about 1920 pixels wide for a laptop and 3840 for a 4K monitor.

At capture: shoot at the camera’s full resolution, avoid digital zoom (walk closer instead), and send photos as files or links rather than through apps that shrink them.

Blur comes in two kinds. Motion blur smears edges in one direction, because the camera or the subject moved. Focus blur makes everything uniformly soft, because the camera focused on the wrong thing or the lens was dirty.

A “sharpen” slider only boosts contrast at edges. It makes a slightly soft photo crisper, but on real blur it adds halos without bringing back detail. For real blur, use a model that reconstructs it:

Be realistic about severe blur. When a face or a line of text is too blurred to read, any AI model has to invent the detail. The result can look sharp and still be wrong, so compare it with the original, especially for faces, license plates and documents.

At capture: clean the lens (a fingerprint smear is the most common cause of soft phone photos), hold the phone with both hands or brace it on something, tap the subject to focus, and use burst mode for moving subjects.

Noise is the colored speckle you see in dark areas of photos taken in low light. The camera raises its sensitivity (ISO) to compensate for the missing light, and the sensor’s random errors become visible. Small phone sensors and digital zoom make it worse.

Lighting problems are the one category where a normal photo editor is usually the right tool. The photo’s information is there; it is just too dark, too bright or the wrong color.

Every phone gallery app and every desktop editor has these four controls. If you want a different look rather than a correction, such as studio light or golden hour, Krea’s change lighting tool relights a photo from a text description.

At capture: put the light source in front of your subject, not behind them, turn on HDR for scenes with bright sky and dark foreground, and avoid on-camera flash at close range.

Every time a JPEG is saved, or a photo passes through a messaging app or social platform, it is compressed again. The signs are blocky 8 × 8 squares in smooth areas, halos around edges, and banding in skies.

Upload a low-resolution, noisy or compressed photo and the Krea Enhancer upscales and cleans it up in seconds. A limited number of enhancements are free without an account.

Video has the same five problems, multiplied by every frame, and frame-by-frame photo tools produce flicker. Use a video model instead: Krea’s video upscaler takes an MP4 and lets you pick 1x, 2x, 4x or 8x, depending on the source resolution and your plan. It needs a signed-in account, and free users can enhance up to 4 videos every 24 hours.

At capture, the same rules apply: clean the lens, add light, lock focus and exposure, and record at the highest resolution and frame rate your phone offers.
